newsitem.title: USA: White House condemns blast in Northern Ireland.
newsitem.headline: White House condemns blast in Northern Ireland.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday condemned in the strongest terms Monday's bombing of British Army headquarters in Northern Ireland, but said these "acts of terrorism" should not be allowed to derail the peace process.

White House press secretary Mike McCurry, referring to the IRA's admission to the bombing in Lisburn, near Belfast, also said the United States hoped these "men of violence" would be brought to justice.
"The United States condemns in the strongest terms yesterday's barbaric attack on the military base at Lisburn in Northern Ireland, which injured over 30 people," McCurry said in a statement.

"Now the Irish Republican Army has claimed responsibility for this deadly criminal act. These men of violence are acting against the interests and hopes of the people of Ireland, North and South, who want a just and lasting peace," he said.

McCurry continued, saying: "These acts of terrorism must not be allowed to derail the important work of peace occurring in Belfast under the chairmanship of Senator (George) Mitchell and his two colleagues."
The United States said it stood with the British and Irish governments in their determination to press forward with the peace negotiations.
McCurry also underscored U.S. support for the "courage and determination the loyalists have shown in resisting provocation and refusing to be drawn into the spiral of violence."
British Prime Minister John Major led a chorus of calls on Tuesday to Loyalist guerrillas not to avenge the IRA attack on the Lisburn army base but to abide by a two-year ceasefire.

The Loyalists' umbrella organisation, the Combined Loyalist Military Command, made no statement after a meeting on Tuesday, raising tensions among the 40 percent Catholic minority and 60 percent Protestant majority alike.

The IRA statement, admitting its guerrillas carried out the bombing of Britain's army headquarters in Lisburn, south of Belfast, appeared to signal the start of a new campaign in Northern Ireland itself after a two-year respite.
The attack humiliated British security, wounded 20 soldiers and 11 civilians, and was the most audacious IRA strike since the guerrillas fired mortars into Heathrow airport in 1994.
Since ending its own 17-month ceasefire in February, the IRA has struck targets in British cities and a British army base in Germany but has avoided attacking Northern Ireland itself.
